methodology.title: Behind the data
methodology.description: Where the events come from, how they're shown, and where they fall short

source.title: One source: Wikipedia
source.p1: Every event comes from Wikipedia's “On this day” service, which gathers each day's anniversaries. Our server queries it, not your browser. We don't add, remove or rewrite entries: you see what Wikipedia lists for that day, with links to the articles it mentions.
source.p2: Entries come in five kinds: Featured, a short selection curated by Wikipedia's volunteers; Events; Births; Deaths; Holidays and observances.

report.title: Today's report
report.intro: What our server returned for today, {{date}}: real data, the same the map and the Dashboard use.
report.caption: Sections received for today, {{date}}
report.warningPrimaryUnavailable: Today the edition in the requested language didn't respond: every section comes from the other one.
report.warningFallbackUnavailable: Today a section missing in the requested language couldn't be filled in from the other one either.
report.footnote: The map and the Dashboard use only these two sections. Births, deaths and holidays are in the <archive>Archive</archive>.

languages.title: Languages
languages.p1: Texts are requested in the interface language when the service offers it, which here means Italian or English only. With the interface in German or French, texts arrive in English.
languages.p2: The Italian edition publishes no births or deaths: when Italian is requested, those two sections come from the English one, and the page says so. If the requested edition doesn't respond, everything comes from the other. In the <archive>Archive</archive> you can pick the text language yourself.

freshness.title: Updates
freshness.p1: A day's copy is reused for six hours before Wikipedia is asked again. If Wikipedia doesn't respond, we show the last saved copy, at most seven days old, marked “Data may be out of date”.

geocoding.title: The country on the map
geocoding.p1: Wikipedia doesn't say which country an event happened in, so we infer it. We take the first linked article that has coordinates and look up the country containing that point, on Natural Earth's 1:110 million borders.
geocoding.p2: It's an approximation, with specific limits:
geocoding.limitSubject: coordinates describe the article's subject, not always where the event took place;
geocoding.limitNone: an event with no linked article carrying coordinates gets no country: it's in the day's list, but isn't counted on the map;
geocoding.limitBorder: a point near a border can land in the neighboring country;
geocoding.limitIslands: some small island states have no shape at this scale and are never identified.
geocoding.p3: Only Events count on the map: Featured repeats some of them, and counting them twice would inflate the numbers.

index.title: The country index
index.p1: The <century>My century</century> page uses an index our server builds every night: it reads every day of the year in Italian and English and places each event in a country with the same rule and the same borders as the map. It holds only Events with a year and an identified country, each edition on its own (no fallback between languages), and can be a day behind Wikipedia.

errors.title: Contradictions and errors
errors.p1: With a single source there's nothing to reconcile: we don't check entries against other archives. A mistake in an event's text is fixed on Wikipedia, on the page for that day of the year; the correction reaches this site with the next update.
errors.p2: For this site's own mistakes, such as a wrongly attributed country, write to us via <credits>Credits and contact</credits>.

limits.title: Limits
limits.p1: Coverage is Wikipedia's, which isn't even across countries and eras. Entries run from antiquity to the present, not just the 20th century. The numbers on the map and the Dashboard describe today's entries, not history as a whole.

views.title: Visit statistics
views.p1: “Most viewed”, on the Dashboard, are anonymous totals: a day is counted each time its events are requested, a country each time it's selected. No personal data and no visitor identifier; details are on the <privacy>Privacy</privacy> page (in Italian).

guide.title: How to use
guide.description: Short answers for reading the map, looking up a day and adjusting the site

map.title: What does the map show?
map.p1: Events that happened on this date in past years, country by country. The color shows how many of today's events were attributed to each country:
map.p2: A country without color has no events attributed today, which doesn't mean nothing happened there. How the country is inferred is explained in <methodology>Behind the data</methodology>.

country.title: How do I see a country's events?
country.p1: Click the country on the map, or pick it from “Go to a country” in the events panel: the <kbd>/</kbd> key takes you straight there. To return to all of today's events, use the X at the top of the panel.

archive.title: How do I look up another day?
archive.p1: In the <archive>Archive</archive>: choose the month and day, then narrow by years (negative before the common era, e.g. -44), entry type and language. The search box filters that day's entries.

theme.title: Can I follow a country or a topic across the year?
theme.p1: A country, yes: <century>My century</century> shows all its events from the year in time order. For a topic such as the Cold War the archive works one day at a time: set the years 1947 to 1991, search for a word like “Berlin”, then change the day.

dashboard.title: What does the Dashboard measure?
dashboard.p1: Figures computed from today's entries: how many events, in how many countries, the span of years they cover and the most-cited country. Below, the most-viewed days and countries, counted anonymously.

language.title: Why aren't the texts always in my language?
language.p1: Wikipedia's service is available here only in Italian and English: with the interface in German or French, texts arrive in English. The Italian edition, for its part, lacks births and deaths, which come from the English one, marked as such. You can pick the text language in the Archive; more in <methodology>Behind the data</methodology>.

stale.title: What does “Data may be out of date” mean?
stale.p1: That Wikipedia couldn't be reached: you're seeing the last saved copy, at most seven days old. It updates by itself once Wikipedia responds again.

shortcuts.title: Are there keyboard shortcuts?
shortcuts.p1: Yes: <kbd>1</kbd>, <kbd>2</kbd>, <kbd>3</kbd>, <kbd>4</kbd> and <kbd>5</kbd> open Map, Dashboard, Archive, My century and Settings; <kbd>/</kbd> jumps to the country picker. They don't work while you're typing in a field. The list is also in <settings>Settings</settings>.

prefs.title: Where are my preferences saved?
prefs.p1: Only in your browser: theme, language, map projection, reduced motion, and whether you've seen the welcome page. You can clear them from <settings>Settings</settings>; details are on the <privacy>Privacy</privacy> page (in Italian).

data.commons: Images: <commons>Wikimedia Commons</commons>. Each image has its own license, stated on the file page linked next to it.
data.photo: Photo on the 404 error page: O.G. Rejlander, 1872, <photo>Wellcome Collection</photo>, CC BY 4.0 license.

software.title: Software
software.p1: The code is open source under the MIT license: <frontend>the interface</frontend> and <backend>the services</backend> are on GitHub. It's built on free projects such as React, MapLibre GL and Spring Boot.
software.p2: Typefaces: Oswald and Source Serif 4, under the SIL Open Font License.

thanks.title: Thanks
thanks.p1: To the volunteer communities of Wikipedia, Wikimedia Commons, OpenStreetMap and Natural Earth, who make this data free, and to the maintainers of the free software this site stands on.

contact.title: Contact and collaboration

contact.p2: A mistake in an event's text is fixed directly on Wikipedia, on the page for that day of the year; the correction reaches this site with the next update.
